chapterNote: David's psalm about keeping his mouth shut, and what happened when he could not. He set a guard on his tongue because the wicked were watching and he would not hand them ammunition; so he went dumb, silent even from good — and the pain only banked up. His heart got hot; while he mused the fire caught; and then he spoke, and what came out was not a complaint about his enemies but a question about himself: LORD, make me know my end, the measure of my days, how transient I am. The answers are the Bible's shortest measurements of a life: my days are handbreadths, my lifetime is nothing before You, every man at his firmest is a breath, every man walks about as a shadow, he piles up and does not know who will gather it. Out of that comes the psalm's one anchor — and now, Lord, what do I wait for? My hope is in You — and a plea to be delivered from his transgressions rather than his troubles. He goes silent again, this time because he sees whose hand it is. The last request is startling: look away from me, so that I can smile again before I go and am no more. Jeduthun's choir sang it; the church has read it at gravesides ever since.

1.text: For the choir director, for Jeduthun. A psalm of David. I said, 'I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue; I will keep a muzzle on my mouth as long as the wicked is in front of me.'
1.amp: To the chief Musician [natsach], even to Jeduthun, A Psalm [mizmor] of David. I said [amar], I will take heed [shamar — guard] to my ways [derek], that I sin [chet] not with my tongue [lashon]: I will keep [shamar] my mouth ['a bridle, or, muzzle for my mouth', machsom, the KJV margin] with a bridle [machsom — muzzle], while the wicked [rasha] is before me.
1.notes: amarti eshmerah derakhai me-chato bi-lshoni (H559, H8104, H1870, H2398, H3956): I said I would GUARD my ways from sinning with my tongue — eshmerah le-phi machsom (H6310, H4269): I will keep a machsom for my mouth, the margin's 'muzzle': the strap put on an animal's jaws. be-od rasha le-negdi (H7563): while the wicked is in front of me — the reason for the muzzle is an audience, not a principle. Jeduthun (H3038) was one of David's three chief musicians (1 Chronicles 25:1).

2.text: I was mute and still; I kept quiet even from good, and my pain was stirred up.
2.amp: I was dumb [alam] with silence, I held my peace [chashah], even from good [tov]; and my sorrow was stirred ['troubled', akar, the KJV margin].
2.notes: neelamti dumiyyah hechesheti mi-tov (H481, H1747, H2814, H2896): I was struck mute in silence; I kept still even from GOOD — the silence overshot: he stopped saying the true things along with the rash ones; u-kebi nekar (H3511, H5916): and my pain was stirred, the margin's 'troubled'. Bottled grief does not stay level; it builds.

3.text: My heart grew hot inside me; as I mused the fire kept burning; then I spoke with my tongue:
3.amp: My heart [leb] was hot [chamam] within [qereb] me, while I was musing the fire [esh] burned [baar]: then [az] spoke [dabar] I with my tongue [lashon],
3.notes: cham-libbi be-qirbi (H2552, H3820, H7130): my heart grew HOT inside me — ba-hagigi tibar-esh (H1901, H1197, H784): in my musing the fire kept burning — hagig, from the same root as the muttering of Psalm 1:2; dibbarti bi-lshoni (H1696, H3956): I spoke with my tongue. The muzzle comes off, and what comes out is the rest of the psalm — addressed not to the wicked but to God, which is why the silence was worth breaking (cf. Luke 24:32's burning heart).

4.text: 'LORD, make me know my end and the measure of my days, what it is; let me know how transient I am.
4.amp: LORD [YHWH], make me to know [yada] mine end [qets], and the measure [middah] of my days [yom], what it is; that I may know [yada] how frail ['what time I have here', chadel, the KJV margin] I am.
4.notes: hodieni YHWH qitsi u-middat yamai mah-hi (H3045, H3068, H7093, H4060, H3117): make me KNOW my end and the measure of my days, what it is — edeah meh-chadel ani (H2310): let me know how chadel I am: how ceasing, how transient, the margin's 'what time I have here'. The strangest prayer in the Psalter, and the sanest: he asks not for more days but for the number of them (cf. Psalm 90:12).

5.text: Look — You have made my days handbreadths, and my lifetime is as nothing before You; surely every man, however firmly he stands, is only a breath. Selah.
5.amp: Behold, You have made [natan] my days [yom] as an handbreadth; and mine age [cheled — lifetime] is as nothing before You: verily every [kol] man [adam] at his best state ['settled', natsab, the KJV margin] is altogether [kol] vanity [hebel — a breath]. Selah [Selah].
5.notes: hinneh tephachot natattah yamai (H2947, H5414, H3117): You have made my days handbreadths — the width of four fingers, the shortest measure in the Hebrew toolkit; ve-cheldi khe-ayin negdekha (H2465): and my cheled, my lifetime, is as nothing in front of You; akh kol-hebel kol-adam nitsab (H1892, H120, H5324): surely every man STANDING FIRM — the margin's 'settled' — is entirely hebel, a breath: Ecclesiastes' word, thirty-eight times in that book and here in a psalm. Selah, on a handbreadth.

6.text: Surely a man goes about as a shadow; surely they are in an uproar over nothing; he heaps up and does not know who will gather it.
6.amp: Surely every man [ish] walks [halak] in a vain shew ['an image', tselem, the KJV margin]: surely they are disquieted [hamah] in vain [hebel — a breath]: he heaps up riches, and knows [yada] not who shall gather [asaph] them.
6.notes: akh be-tselem yithallekh-ish (H6754, H1980, H376): a man walks about in a tselem — the margin's 'image', the word for the image of God in Genesis 1:27, here meaning a mere semblance, a shadow-shape; akh-hebel yehemayun (H1892, H1993): surely for a breath they ROAR — hamah, the noise of a crowd or a sea; yitsbor ve-lo-yeda mi-osepham (H6651, H3045, H622): he piles up and does not know who will GATHER it — the rich fool's question (Luke 12:20), asked a thousand years early.

7.text: 'So now, Lord, what am I waiting for? You — You are my hope.
7.amp: And now, Lord [Adonai], what wait [qavah] I for? my hope is in You.
7.notes: ve-attah mah-qivviti Adonai (H6960, H136): and now — what have I WAITED for, Lord? qavah, the tension-word, hope as a cord pulled taut (Isaiah 40:31); tochalti lekha hi (H8431): my hope, it is in You. The pivot of the psalm: after the handbreadth and the shadow, the only thing left standing is the One the days are measured against.

8.text: Rescue me from every one of my transgressions; do not set me up as the fool's taunt.
8.amp: Deliver [natsal] me from all my transgressions [pesha]: make [sum] me not the reproach [cherpah] of the foolish [nabal].
8.notes: mi-kol-peshaai hatsileni (H6588, H5337): from ALL my transgressions rescue me — the request is not for health or years but for pardon; cherpat nabal al-tesimeni (H2781, H5036, H7760): do not make me the taunt of the nabal, the moral fool of Psalm 14:1. The wicked man of verse 1 is still watching; David asks God to make sure he has nothing to see.

9.text: I stayed mute and would not open my mouth, because this was Your doing.
9.amp: I was dumb [alam], I opened [pathach] not my mouth [peh]; because You did [asah] it.
9.notes: neelamti lo ephtach-pi (H481, H6605, H6310): I was struck mute, I do not open my mouth — verse 2's silence again, but for a wholly different reason: ki attah asita (H6213): because YOU did it. The first silence was tactical, to deny his enemies a quotation; this one is worship, and it is the same silence as Aaron's (Leviticus 10:3) and Job's (Job 40:4-5).

10.text: Take Your stroke away from me; I am finished off by the hostility of Your hand.
10.amp: Remove [sur] Your stroke [nega] away [sur] from me: I am consumed [kalah] by the blow ['conflict', tigrah, the KJV margin] of Your hand [yad].
10.notes: haser me-alai nigekha (H5493, H5061): REMOVE Your nega from me — the stroke of Psalm 38:11, the leprosy-examination word; mi-tigrat yadekha ani khaliti (H8409, H3027, H3615): from the tigrah of Your hand — the margin's 'conflict', a hostility, an attack — I am finished. Silent submission (v. 9) and asking for it to stop are not contradictions; this psalm does both in consecutive verses.

11.text: With rebukes for iniquity You discipline a man, and You melt away what he treasures like a moth; surely every man is a breath. Selah.
11.amp: When You with rebukes [tokachat] correct [yasar — discipline] man [ish] for iniquity [avon], You make his beauty ['that which is to be desired in him to melt away', chamad, the KJV margin] to consume away like a moth: surely every man [adam] is vanity [hebel — a breath]. Selah [Selah].
11.notes: be-tokhachot al-avon yissarta ish (H8433, H5771, H3256, H376): with rebukes over iniquity You discipline a man; va-temes ka-ash chamudo (H4529, H6211, H2530): and You MELT, like a moth does, 'that which is to be desired in him' — the margin's literal: whatever a man has that is precious, thinned out like wool eaten from the inside (cf. Hosea 5:12; Matthew 6:19-20); akh hebel kol-adam (H1892, H120): surely every man is a breath — verse 5's refrain, now with the moth in it. Selah.

12.text: 'Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry reach Your ear; do not go silent at my tears. For with You I am a guest, a lodger passing through, as every one of my fathers was.
12.amp: Hear [shama] my prayer [tephillah], O LORD [YHWH], and give ear [azan] unto my cry; hold not Your peace [charash] at my tears: for I am a stranger [ger — resident alien] with You, and a sojourner [toshab], as all my fathers [ab] were.
12.notes: shimah-tephillati YHWH ve-shavati haazinah (H8085, H8605, H3068, H238): hear my prayer, give ear to my cry — el-dimati al-techerash (H1832, H2790): at my tears do not be DEAF-SILENT — charash, the silence Psalm 28:1 dreaded; ki ger anokhi immakh toshab ke-khol-abotai (H1616, H8453, H1): for I am a ger with You, a toshab — resident alien and temporary lodger, the exact legal pair Abraham used at Machpelah (Genesis 23:4) and Leviticus 25:23 uses of Israel on God's land. The whole race lives on someone else's property; Hebrews 11:13 makes it a confession.

13.text: Look away from me, so that I may recover a smile, before I go and am no more.'
13.amp: O spare [shaah — look away] me, that I may recover strength [balag], before I go hence [yalak], and be no more.
13.notes: hasha mimmenni ve-abligah (H8159, H1082): LOOK AWAY from me and let me brighten — balag, to gleam, to cheer up: the one prayer in Scripture that asks God to stop looking, the reverse of the Aaronic blessing's shining face, because this face has been burning (v. 10); be-terem elekh ve-eneni (H3212): before I go and am not. Job prays the same thing (Job 10:20-21; 14:6). The psalm ends without resolution — which is why the church has kept it for gravesides, where none is available yet.
